title: Family Car
hook: How an ordinary car works: four pistons on a crankshaft, a gearbox, a propshaft and a differential.
summary: For most of the twentieth century a car was built like this: an engine at the front, burning petrol in four cylinders, and its power taken back to the rear wheels through a clutch, a gearbox, a long propshaft and a differential in the rear axle. This one is of no particular make, a family saloon of the 1970s or 80s, but its parts are the ones almost every car of the time had.

In the engine, four pistons are pushed down in turn by burning petrol and air, and their connecting rods turn the crankshaft. A camshaft, driven by a toothed belt at half the crankshaft’s speed, opens each cylinder’s valves at the right moment of its four strokes. The gearbox trades speed for pulling power, and the differential lets the rear wheels turn at different speeds in a bend.
This model was built in code for this site; its sizes are those of a typical saloon of the time.

parts.label: Crankshaft
parts.about: Turns the pistons’ up and down into turning: a crankpin for each rod with a counterweight opposite, the flywheel at the back.

parts.label: Intake
parts.about: Air comes in through the filter and along the runners, petrol is added, and the mixture goes into the cylinders.

parts.label: Battery
parts.about: Twelve volts for the starter motor, the sparks and the lights.

parts.label: Propshaft
parts.about: Takes the drive back from the gearbox to the rear axle, with a universal joint at each end so the axle can move on its springs.

parts.label: Gearbox
parts.about: Four forward gears in a cast case; the lever moves the selectors inside.

parts.label: Gears
parts.about: The input shaft drives the layshaft below it; the layshaft’s gears drive a gear for each speed, turning freely on the main shaft until one is locked to it.

parts.label: Clutch
parts.about: Springs press its disc against the flywheel; pressing the pedal lets it go, to change gear or to stop.

parts.label: Rear axle
parts.about: The axle’s casing: the differential in its middle, the half shafts in its tubes.

parts.label: Differential
parts.about: The pinion turns the crown wheel and the carrier with it; the spider gears in the carrier share the drive between the two half shafts.

parts.label: Half shafts
parts.about: From the differential out to the wheels, inside the axle’s tubes.

parts.label: Rear springs
parts.about: Leaf springs and dampers: the axle hangs from the body on them.

parts.label: Front suspension
parts.about: At each front corner, two wishbones hold the wheel’s upright, with a coil spring round the damper; the steering rack turns the uprights.

how.label: Layout
how.title: From the engine to the rear wheels
text: The engine at the front makes the power. It goes back through the clutch and the gearbox, along the propshaft under the floor, and into the rear axle, where the differential turns it through a right angle and out along the half shafts to the wheels.
A car like this carries its own fuel and has to cool itself: the tank is under the boot, the radiator in the nose, the exhaust runs the length of the car, and a battery starts it all.

chart.title: Where the petrol’s energy goes
chart.caption: Rough shares at a steady speed: only about a quarter of the energy in the fuel ends up turning the wheels.

how.label: Four strokes
how.title: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow
text: Each cylinder works in four strokes, two turns of the crankshaft. The piston goes down with the intake valve open, drawing in air and petrol; comes up with both valves shut, squeezing them; the spark plug fires and the burning mixture drives it down, the only stroke that does any work; and it comes up again with the exhaust valve open, pushing the burnt gas out.

The four cylinders fire in the order 1, 3, 4, 2, one every half turn, so one of them is always on its power stroke. The camshaft turns once for every two turns of the crankshaft, and its lobes open each valve at its moment.

chart.title: The four strokes, cylinder by cylinder
chart.caption: Each line is a piston’s height, cylinders 1 to 4 from the front, through one turn of the camshaft. They fire 1, 3, 4, 2, so a power stroke starts every half turn of the crank.

how.label: Gearbox
how.title: Gears for pulling, and for speed
text: An engine only works well over a band of speeds, so the gearbox lets it turn faster than the wheels when the car needs to pull (in first, three and a half turns of the engine for each turn of the propshaft) and at the same speed when it cruises (in fourth, the input and the output locked together).

All the gears are always in mesh. The layshaft below is driven by the input shaft, and its gears drive one gear for each speed, turning freely on the main shaft; choosing a gear locks that one to the shaft. Pick a gear and watch the propshaft.

speeds.label: 1st
speeds.note: 3.5 turns of the engine for one of the propshaft

speeds.label: 4th
speeds.note: Direct: the input and the output locked together

chart.title: Engine turns for each turn of the propshaft
chart.caption: In first the engine turns three and a half times for each turn of the propshaft, so the wheels get three and a half times its pull.

how.label: Differential
how.title: Letting the wheels turn at different speeds
text: In a bend the outside wheel travels further than the inside one, so it has to turn faster. The propshaft’s pinion turns the crown wheel and the carrier with it; in the carrier, the spider gears drive the half shafts’ gears. Straight ahead the spiders don’t turn and both shafts go round with the carrier; in a bend the spiders roll round, and one shaft gains what the other loses.
The pinion has ten teeth and the crown wheel thirty-nine: the last reduction between the engine and the wheels, 3.9 to 1.

speeds.label: Straight
speeds.note: Both wheels at the carrier’s speed; the spider gears still

speeds.label: Bend left
speeds.note: The right wheel outside, faster; the left one slower

speeds.label: Bend right
speeds.note: The left wheel outside, faster; the right one slower

chart.title: The two wheels and the crown wheel
chart.caption: The dials turn with the half shafts and the crown wheel: in a bend, the outside wheel runs ahead of the crown wheel by as much as the inside one falls behind.

how.label: Cooling
how.title: Throwing heat away
text: Burning petrol in the cylinders makes far more heat than work, and the engine would seize without a way to get rid of it. Water is pumped round passages in the block and the head, then through the radiator in the nose, where the air coming through the grille (and pulled by the fan) cools it.
About as much of the fuel’s energy goes into the radiator as goes out of the exhaust, and each of them is more than turns the wheels.
